title: Chapter 126 – Wenyuan's Council
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Wenyuan]

Lin Wenyuan wakes before the cock, as he has every morning for sixty-three years, and lies in the dark counting mouths.

It is a habit older than the clan. When he was a boy in the Orchard, the count had been four: his father, his mother, his sister, himself. When he married Qinghe it was six. When the Orchard fell it was a bare handful of survivors on a cart, and the count was the first thing he did each dawn to be sure he had not lost another in the night. Now it is a different sum. He lies on his back with his hands folded and his wife's slow breath at his shoulder, and he lets the numbers rise in his head like water in a well.

Four hundred and thirty.

Four hundred and thirty people sleep under the Garden's roofs this morning. Eleven were born since the spring. Nineteen came in from the lower villages, field hands and weavers and a family of stone-cutters who heard that the Lin clan paid in grain and kept its word. Six came from the Orchard roll itself, old men who had been thought dead, who walked in out of the dust with their hands out and their names on their lips. He had wept at every one. He is not ashamed of it.

Four hundred and thirty, and eleven in the ground since the siege, and seven who will never again hold a hoe.

"You are counting," says Qinghe, into the pillow.

"I am resting."

"Your lips are moving."

"They are resting too."

She turns over. In the gray light her face is lined and small and shrewd, with the stubborn jaw of a woman who has outlived three famines. She is sixty-one and her hair has gone the color of ash. "Is it the council?"

"It is always the council."

"Then eat first." She sits up, finds her slippers with her toes, and stands with a small grunt, one hand on the bedpost. "Men who decide on empty stomachs vote for wars."

* * *

The Garden Hall, on council mornings, smells of boiled barley and wet wool and the sharp green of crushed mint, because Qinghe believes that a quarrel goes easier on a mouth that is busy.

The long table has been dragged into the center of the floor. Seven chairs for the Garden council, and another dozen along the walls for those who must be heard and do not vote. The shutters are open, and the cold light from the terraces falls across the board in long clean strips. Wenyuan takes his place at the head, not in the high chair, which he has never liked, but in the plain stool at the corner, so that his knees will not show.

They come in, one at a time, and sit.

Hu, first, the one-armed forge-master, with his tool-arm folded on the table like a hammer at rest. He was a drunkard once. He has been sober three hundred and ninety days and counts them as Wenyuan counts mouths. Beside him Wenqing, thin and exact, who keeps the grain-books. Wenshi, his brother, round and gentle, who keeps everyone's feelings. Feng, broad as a door, with a bandage across his knuckles because he has been teaching the younger men to hold a staff. Then two elected members from the lower terraces, a weaver named Pan and a stooped old herdsman called Dull Gu, who has never been known to say more than eight words in a row.

And at the foot of the table, small and upright, with a thick black ledger open in front of her, Yue.

"You have been writing," says Wenyuan.

"I have been counting," his daughter says. "Doors."

There is a faint stir of amusement. She pays it no mind. She turns the ledger one page and lays her finger on a column of tiny characters.

"There are two hundred and eleven doors in the Garden that do not close correctly," she says. "When the new roofs went up in the autumn, the carpenters hung them by sight. They are all a hair off true. Pebble says each one is a seam, and each seam is a way in." Her voice is level. "If the clan is going to be a Seat, it must be a Seat that cannot be opened from the inside."

"Yue," says Hu, gently. "We have not voted to be a Seat."

"We will," says Yue.

* * *

The decree of the Sect Council lies in the middle of the table, under a stone.

It is a long scroll in the Treasury's heavy hand, sealed in white and blue wax, and Wenyuan has read it eleven times. He can recite it. To the Lin of the Garden, by the favor of the Elder Council and in recognition of service rendered at the Siege of the Gate: that the Garden Hall shall be accounted a Seat of the Sect, with a voice in the Hall of Elders; that its tithe be halved for twelve years; that it hold in trust the wall of the Gate Stair; that it send three disciples yearly to the Inner Court; and that its head be named in the Roll of Seats, and answerable.

And answerable. He keeps coming back to those two words.

"It is a good offer," says Wenqing, who has a mind like a measuring cup. "Better than we deserved. The tithe alone will feed sixty more mouths."

"It is a leash," says Hu.

"It is a leash with a bowl of food at the end of it."

"Every leash has one."

"Stop," says Wenshi softly. "Both of you. We are not enemies."

Wenyuan folds his hands. He has the knack, learned over decades of village feuds, of letting a quarrel run until it is empty, and then saying one plain thing into the silence. He waits. Dull Gu coughs. A sparrow lands on the sill, looks at the room, and decides against it.

"Who would we answer to?" he asks.

The table stops.

"I mean it. Who? The Elders? There are nine of them, and three are the Treasury's creatures, and two will not see sixty. The Council? It is a room full of men who rushed to give us a Seat the morning after we won a war they did not fight. I do not say they are wicked. I say they are useful, and we are useful to them, and that is a very different thing from being loved." He turns his wide, weathered hands over. "A Seat is a debt. Not tomorrow. Not this year. But it is the sort of debt that sleeps in a drawer until the day you can least afford to pay."

"Then we decline," says Feng.

"We could."

"But?"

"But we have four hundred and thirty mouths," says Wenyuan. "And a Seat feeds them."

Nobody has an answer.

It is Dull Gu who breaks it, to everyone's astonishment, in a voice like a hinge. "My father farmed a lord's field," he says. "And my father's father. Always rented. Always answerable. I have wished all my life to own a hill, and now I may own one, and it is a hill with a chain on it." He scratches his ear. "Well. I have been on worse hills."

That is eight words. He sits back, flushed, and says nothing more for the rest of the day.

* * *

They vote in the early afternoon, by dropping pebbles in a bowl.

White for the Seat, black against. Qinghe has brought the bowl herself, an old cracked thing with a blue rim that came from the Orchard on the cart, and she holds it out to each of them in turn, with her face blank, so that none can see how another casts. It rattles. It rattles again. Six pebbles drop.

Wenyuan counts them, upturned on the table.

Five white. One black.

"The black is mine," says Hu, without shame. "I want it understood. I will carry the Seat as well as any man. But someone at this table must always have voted against."

"Noted," says Wenyuan, and means it.

The seventh stone is the head's, and he holds it in his palm for a long moment. It is white. It is warm from his hand. He thinks of the Orchard, of the cart, of the dust. He thinks of his son, standing in a green-lit stair with his hand on a wall, who has not asked for anything in thirty-six years and has not once complained. He drops it in the bowl.

"The Seat is accepted," he says. "And its head?"

"Yue," says Qinghe.

The room turns.

"I have said it before, and I say it now. I have watched my daughter keep a ledger of doors for eight years, and I have watched this council wave her away as a clever girl with a pet." Qinghe's voice is steady, but her knuckles are white on the bowl. "She has no root. The Mirror said so. And she has heard the seams of this house since she was a child, and kept it from more harm than all our elders. If we are a Seat, we are a Seat that must be kept. I will not have it kept by anyone but her."

"It is not for me to say," Yue whispers.

"It is exactly for you to say," says her mother. "That is why we are asking."

Yue looks at the ledger. She looks at her father. She looks at Pebble, who has jumped onto the corner of the table and is sitting in the sun with her tail around her feet, ears forward.

"If I hold it," she says slowly, "I hold it as a door. Not as a throne. When Jian comes home, he opens it. When he goes, he closes it. And if ever I am asked to open it to the wrong person, I will not."

"That is what a head is," says Wenyuan, and his voice cracks. "Welcome, daughter."

* * *

Feng finds him on the upper terrace afterward, leaning on a drystone wall and looking at the valley as if it owed him money.

His elder son is forty-three and a Foundation Establishment cultivator in the Middle stage, which in the Sect's reckoning makes him a minor prodigy and in his own a man who has not yet done anything. He sits down on the wall with his legs dangling like a boy's. The bandage on his knuckles has begun to fray.

"You voted yes."

"I did."

"I would have voted no." Feng picks at a loose thread. "Not because it is wrong. Because it frightens me. We have spent thirty-five years being small enough to ignore. I do not want to be a thing the Elders look at."

"You are already a thing they look at."

"Then I do not want it written down."

Wenyuan smiles. It is the tired, fond smile of a man who has been having this conversation, in one form or another, since his first child learned to walk. "What do you want, Feng?"

His son is silent for a time. A hawk drifts over the ridge, turning on the cold air.

"To be strong enough that it does not matter," he says at last. "I have been Middle for four years. Jian is nine steps above me. He is thirty-six and he is Purple Mansion, and he does not boast of it, and he does not rest, and I lie in bed at night and think, I am the elder brother. I am supposed to be the wall." His jaw works. "I am the wall's cousin."

"A wall is not a thing you are. It is a thing you do."

"Say that to my knuckles."

"I will say it to your mother, who will say it to you louder." Wenyuan puts a cold hand on his son's shoulder, and Feng flinches, and then, slowly, leans into it. "You will break through, Feng. Not tonight. Not this year. But Bai says the Garden has a Purple Mansion pill in its future, and your brother has a way of finding what we need. When the day comes, you will be ready. A man who has been practicing to be a wall for four years does not forget the shape."

"And if I am not?"

"Then we will be a family with a very stubborn eldest son," says Wenyuan. "I have survived worse."

Feng laughs, once, rough. He wipes his nose on his wrist and says nothing more. They sit together a while longer on the cold wall, two broad men looking at the same valley, until the light begins to go.

* * *

Hu catches him at the forge door on his way back, and does not let him pass.

The one-armed artifact refiner, stands in the red glow with his tool-arm folded and his good hand wrapped round a cup of hot barley water. Behind him the fire crackles, the bellows sigh, and a half-made hinge hangs on a hook like a question.

"I want a word."

"You have had eleven."

"I want a twelfth." Hu's blunt face is ruddy. "I voted against. I told you I would, and I did, and I will again, the next time you ask us to take a gift from a man who calls himself our friend. But I want you to know why."

"I know why."

"You do not." Hu lowers his voice. "I was a drunk. You know that. You carried me home on your back when I could not stand, and you put me to bed, and you said nothing about it in the morning. Nothing. Not once in three hundred and ninety days." He swallows. "That is the only reason I am alive. Not Jian's tool-arm. Not the Garden. That."

"Hu—"

"Let me finish. A man who has been carried does not like to see the carrier pulled by a chain. I voted against the leash because you taught me what it is to be held up by something that asked nothing. And now you are going to hold up four hundred and thirty people with a chain on your own neck." He sets down the cup. "I would rather you did not. But if you do, I will be at your back with a hammer. That is all."

Wenyuan looks at him for a long moment. Then he opens his cold hands, and takes the bigger man's good hand in both of them, and holds it.

"Thank you," he says, "for being the black stone."

"It was no trouble," says Hu, gruffly. "I keep a few handy."

* * *

The cold comes up through the floor at dusk.

He has been feeling it for a week. Not the weather: something in the bones. The Foundation Establishment breath that he carries in his lower belly, which he earned in a siege at sixty-two with a stranger's pill and a son's blood, has begun to flicker. It was a bright flame when he first lit it. Now it gutters, as though a draft had found a crack. He has said nothing. A man who has been told all his life to keep his troubles to himself finds it hard to unlearn.

It is Qinghe who knows.

She finds him in the kitchen after the council, scraping the barley pot, and takes the spoon from his hand and says, "Sit."

"I am well."

"You have been well for a week. You have been well so long that you have started to lean on the wall." She puts her hands on his face. They are small hands, work-cracked, very warm. "Wenyuan. I have been married to you for forty-one years. Do you think I do not feel when you are afraid?"

"I am not afraid."

"No. You are ashamed." Her thumbs press gently on his cheekbones. "Of what? That you are old? That your breath is thin? That you must ask?"

"That I must ask him." He cannot meet her eyes. "He is my son. I held him before he could hold his head. He has carried this family on his back for five years, and I am a father, and a father does not hold out his hand."

"A father does what keeps his family alive."

"It is not so simple."

"It is exactly so simple." She lets go. "I told Bai I would go second. I told Jian. I meant it. But I will not watch you go out like a lamp in a draught because you are too proud to say a word to a boy who would cut off his own arm for you." She picks up the spoon and points it at him like a sword. "Ask him. Tonight. Or I will."

* * *

He asks him in the dark, in the back room, under a single lamp.

Jian is waiting. He had known, of course. He always knows. He is sitting cross-legged on the floor with a small lacquered box open before him, and in the box, on a bed of white silk, lies a pill the size of a quail's egg, dull gold, shot through with fine red veins like a leaf in autumn.

"Bone-Marrow Gold," says Jian. "Level three, high grade. Bai made it from the Gate-wall dust and the last of the Fire. It will lift you from Early to Middle."

"What does it cost?"

"Bai says four weeks of pain."

"That is not what I asked."

Jian is silent a moment. He lifts his eyes, and Wenyuan sees in them the thing he has seen more and more in the past few years: a kind of distance, a gaze fixed on something just beyond the wall. His son is looking at the room as one looks at a ledger.

"It costs me a little," says Jian. "The Reservoir. Forty of the fifty-five. It is a number I will earn back."

"How long?"

"Three seasons. Four."

Wenyuan closes his eyes. "And the cost to me?"

"I do not know." The answer comes very quietly. "I have never done it for a man. I only know that every breakthrough has a price, and that it is usually something you did not think to guard."

"Then I will pay it."

"You do not know what it is."

"I know what it is not." Wenyuan opens his eyes and smiles. It is the broad, creased, unguarded smile of a man who has made peace with a decision. "It is not Qinghe. It is not you, and it is not Feng and it is not Yue. Whatever is left, I can bear."

He takes the pill from the box. It is warm in his palm.

* * *

The night is long. He does not remember all of it.

He remembers the taste, bitter-sweet, like burnt honey. He remembers the heat in his belly, and the way it spread, as slowly and surely as ink in water, down his legs and into his arms, until his whole body hummed like a struck bell. He remembers Qinghe's hand in his, and Feng's low voice reading the old counting song, and Pebble's small weight on his chest. He remembers pain, of a sort he has not known since he was beaten as a boy by a tax-collector, a bone-deep, grinding pain, as though his marrow were being melted down and cast again.

And he remembers his son's face, over him, in the lamplight. White and set. Sweating. With one hand pressed flat to Wenyuan's breastbone, and the other fisted so tightly on his knee that the knuckles stood out like pebbles.

At the worst of it, toward the third hour, he hears Jian say, very softly, to nobody, "Hold. Hold. I have you."

Then the pain breaks. It does not fade. It breaks, like a fever, all at once, and he lies on the mat gasping with his heart slamming and his eyes streaming, and he knows with absolute certainty that he is stronger than he was. The flame in his belly is steady. It burns clean and low and deep, and when he breathes in, the air tastes like iron and spring water.

"Middle," he whispers.

"Middle," says Jian.

His son is sitting back on his heels. His face is the color of tallow. A thin line of blood has run from one nostril to his lip, and he does not seem to notice. "Sixty more years, if you are careful. Bai says seventy."

"Seventy." Wenyuan laughs, cracked and breathless. "I will be a hundred and thirty. I will see your children's children."

"Perhaps."

"Perhaps." He raises his hand, to touch his son's shoulder, to say whatever a father says at a time like this, and stops.

His hand is cold.

Not cool: cold. Cold as river stone in January, cold as a dead man's. He turns it over in the lamplight, flexes the fingers. They move. They feel. But under the skin there is no warmth in them at all, nothing, a clean absence. He touches his own cheek with the back of his knuckles and flinches.

"Ah," says Wenyuan.

Jian has seen. His face does not change, but the shadow in his eyes deepens.

"That is the price," Wenyuan says, almost cheerfully. "I wondered what it would be. I had thought perhaps my sense of smell." He closes the hand and opens it. "Well. I have never much liked the cold on my fingers, but a farmer learns to wear gloves."

"Father."

"No." He takes Jian's wrist in his freezing grip, gently, and squeezes. "Listen. It is a small price. I have lived sixty-three years with warm hands, and I have been happy, and if the rest of my life is to be lived with cold ones, I will manage. Your mother will tell me to put them in my armpits, and I will complain, and that will be a very good life." His voice shakes. "Do not carry this one, my son. You carry too much already."

Jian bows his head. He does not answer.

* * *

At dawn, while Qinghe is asleep on the floor with her head against his knee, a boy comes to the Garden gate.

He is not one of theirs. He wears the plain gray of a Registry runner, with a small plum-colored seal sewn over the heart, and he is holding a letter in both hands as though it might bite. Feng meets him at the gate with a staff across his chest, and the boy bows to the staff, to Feng, to the gatepost, and holds out the letter without a word.

It is brought to Wenyuan in the kitchen, still cold from the morning air.

It is a single sheet of heavy paper, the plum-colored paper of the House, sealed with a wafer of the same color. There is no signature. There is only a short message, in a small, formal, courteous hand, that he reads twice, standing by the stove with his cold fingers shaking on the page.

To the Seat of the Garden, upon its establishment, in the name of the House that has known it since the Orchard:

We congratulate you. We would have you know that the Registry does not oppose a Seat of the Lin. On the contrary: we would be honored to enroll it. A House of the Garden, under the House that keeps all Houses, would be spared the Council's tithes, the Elders' leash, and every quarrel that comes with them. We ask only a name. One name, written once.

We will wait.

He sets down the paper. His hands, he notices, have stopped trembling. The cold in them has somehow settled, quiet and absolute, and he feels, for the first time in his life, the exact weight of what his son has been carrying.

Qinghe is standing in the doorway, in her night shawl, with her hair loose.

"What does it say?" she asks.

Wenyuan looks at the letter. He looks at the small plum seal, and the neat hand, and the three words at the end that sit on the page like a stone in a shoe.

"They want to know," he says slowly, "whose name we are going to give them."
